status: candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators

lessons.title: Adding -s, -ed and -ing
lessons.rule: Most words just take the ending. The base word does not change: look → looks, looked, looking.
lessons.tip: Say the base word first, then add the ending you hear.

check.explain: paint + -ing = painting. Nothing changes in paint.

lessons.title: Adding -es
lessons.rule: Words ending in s, x, z, ch or sh add -es, because you can hear an extra syllable: fox → foxes, catch → catches.
lessons.tip: If you can hear an extra 'iz' sound at the end, write -es.

check.explain: church ends in ch, so it takes -es: churches.

lessons.title: Doubling the last letter (short words)
lessons.rule: In a one-syllable word with one short vowel and one final consonant, double the consonant before -ing, -ed, -er or -est: plan → planning, drop → dropped, thin → thinner.

examples.note: not hoped, which comes from hope

lessons.tip: Two consonants keep the vowel short: hopping (short o), hoping (long o).

check.explain: sit has one short vowel and one final consonant, so the t doubles: sitting.

lessons.title: Dropping the silent e
lessons.rule: If a word ends in a silent e, drop the e before an ending that starts with a vowel (-ing, -ed, -er): bake → baking, smile → smiling.
lessons.tip: Keep the e before an ending that starts with a consonant: hope → hopeful.

check.explain: write ends in a silent e, which is dropped before -ing: writing.

lessons.title: Changing y to i
lessons.rule: If a word ends in a consonant + y, change the y to i before -ed, -er, -est or -es: hurry → hurried, funny → funniest, lady → ladies.
lessons.tip: Keep the y before -ing (crying), and after a vowel (play → played).

check.explain: try ends in consonant + y, so the y changes to i: tried.

lessons.title: Doubling in longer words
lessons.rule: In a longer word, double the last consonant only if the last syllable is stressed: permit → permitted, refer → referred.
lessons.tip: Say the word aloud and listen for which syllable is strongest.

check.explain: com-MIT is stressed on the last syllable, so the t doubles: committed.

lessons.title: When not to double
lessons.rule: If the stress is on the first syllable, do not double: limit → limited, enter → entering, offer → offered.
lessons.tip: Compare: preFER → preferred, but OFfer → offered.

check.explain: GAR-den is stressed on the first syllable, so the n does not double: gardening.

lessons.title: Tricky endings
lessons.rule: Three patterns to learn: ie becomes y before -ing (die → dying); add k after a final c (mimic → mimicked); and in British spelling, a final l after one vowel doubles (travel → travelled).
lessons.tip: OpenPath teaches British spelling, and also accepts American spellings as correct.

check.explain: tie ends in ie, which becomes y before -ing: tying.

lessons.title: Adding prefixes and suffixes
lessons.rule: A prefix goes at the start and a suffix at the end. Usually neither part changes: un + happy = unhappy, care + less = careless.
lessons.tip: Spell the two parts separately, then join them.

check.explain: dis + agree = disagree. Nothing is added or dropped.

lessons.title: Double letters where parts join
lessons.rule: When the prefix ends with the same letter the word starts with, keep both: mis + spell = misspell, un + natural = unnatural. The same with -ly after l: real + ly = really.
lessons.tip: A double letter at a join is not a mistake: both parts keep all their letters.

check.explain: un ends in n and necessary starts with n, so both stay: unnecessary.

lessons.title: -ful, -ly and -ment
lessons.rule: The suffix -ful has only one l (hopeful). Adding -ly keeps both parts (careful → carefully). -ment joins without changing the word (move → movement), except argue → argument.
lessons.tip: Full has two l's; the suffix -ful has one.

check.explain: beauty ends in consonant + y, which changes to i, and -ful has one l: beautiful.

lessons.title: -able or -ible
lessons.rule: -able and -ible sound the same. -able usually follows a whole word (read → readable, comfort → comfortable); -ible usually follows a part that is not a word on its own (vis → visible, poss → possible).

examples.note: terr and horr are not words

lessons.tip: It is a guide, not a rule: learn the common -ible words by heart.

check.explain: wash is a whole word, so -able: washable.

lessons.title: -tion, -sion or -ssion
lessons.rule: -tion is the most common ending (station, action). -sion often comes after l, n or r, or makes a 'zh' sound (tension, vision). -ssion often comes from words ending in -ss or -mit (discuss → discussion, permit → permission).
lessons.tip: Think of a related word: discuss → discussion, invade → invasion.

check.explain: discuss ends in -ss, so the noun is discussion.

lessons.title: Long words from roots
lessons.rule: Long words are built from parts. Spell each part: ir + relevant = irrelevant, occasion + al + ly = occasionally, accommodate has two c's and two m's.
lessons.tip: Break a long word into its parts and spell one part at a time.

check.explain: accommodate has a double c and a double m.

lessons.title: Words that sound the same
lessons.rule: Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings: to / two / too, see / sea, son / sun. The meaning of the sentence tells you which one to write.

examples.text: I have two cats. I like cats too. I go to school.
We swam in the sea. I can see you.

lessons.tip: Ask: what does this word mean here?

check.prompt: Which word fits? The ___ is shining.
check.explain: sun is the star in the sky; son is a boy in a family.

lessons.title: there, their and they're
lessons.rule: there = a place (over there; there is). their = belonging to them (their bags). they're = they are. Also: your = belonging to you; you're = you are.

examples.text: They're putting their bags over there.

lessons.tip: Try saying 'they are' or 'you are': if it fits, use the apostrophe.

check.prompt: Which word fits? ___ going to the park.
check.explain: They are going: they're.

lessons.title: its or it's
lessons.rule: it's = it is or it has. its = belonging to it, with no apostrophe (like his and hers).
lessons.tip: Say 'it is'. If it makes sense, write it's; if not, write its.

check.prompt: Which word fits? The cat licked ___ paw.
check.explain: The paw belongs to the cat, so its, with no apostrophe.

lessons.title: Less common sound-alike words
lessons.rule: Some pairs need their meaning learned: whose (belonging to whom) / who's (who is); principal (head, main) / principle (a rule); stationary (not moving) / stationery (paper and pens).

examples.text: Whose bag is this? Who's coming?

lessons.tip: Link one spelling to a memory hook: stationEry, Envelope.

check.prompt: Which word fits? ___ turn is it?
check.explain: The turn belongs to someone: whose.

lessons.title: Words that sound nearly the same
lessons.rule: Some words sound nearly alike: accept (agree to take) / except (but not); lose (not win, not keep) / loose (not tight); advice (a noun) / advise (a verb).

examples.text: Can you give me some advice? I advise you to rest.

lessons.tip: advice and advise: the noun has c, the verb has s.

check.prompt: Which word fits? My shoe is ___.
check.explain: loose means not tight; lose means to stop having something.

lessons.title: Close meanings
lessons.rule: Some pairs are close in meaning: affect is usually a verb (to change something), effect is usually a noun (a result). complement = something that completes; compliment = praise.

examples.text: The rain affected the match. It had a big effect.

lessons.tip: Affect is an Action (verb); Effect is an End result (noun).

check.prompt: Which word fits? The medicine had a strong ___.
check.explain: a strong result: a noun, so effect.

lessons.title: Present simple and regular past
lessons.rule: Use the present simple for habits and facts (I walk to school), and add -ed for most past actions (Yesterday I walked).
lessons.tip: Time words help: every day → present; yesterday, last week → past.

check.prompt: Choose the right verb: Yesterday we ___ to the park.
check.explain: Yesterday tells you it is the past: walked.

lessons.title: Common irregular past forms
lessons.rule: Many common verbs do not take -ed in the past: go → went, buy → bought, see → saw, eat → ate.

examples.text: We went to the market and bought mangoes.
I saw a film and ate popcorn.

lessons.tip: Learn these by heart; never write goed or buyed.

check.prompt: Choose the right verb: She ___ a new bag last week.
check.explain: buy is irregular: bought.

lessons.title: Questions and negatives with did
lessons.rule: After did and didn't, use the base form of the verb: Did you go? I didn't see it. (Not: Did you went?)
lessons.tip: did already shows the past, so the verb stays in its base form.

check.explain: After did, use the base form: see.

lessons.title: Keeping the tense steady
lessons.rule: When you tell a story in the past, keep it in the past: She opened the door and saw a dog. Learn less common irregular forms: catch → caught, choose → chose, lead → led.

examples.text: He caught the ball and threw it back.
They chose a leader who led them well.

lessons.tip: Read your sentences again and check every verb is in the same time.

check.prompt: Choose: The team ___ the cup last year.
check.explain: last year is the past: won.

lessons.title: Uncommon irregular forms
lessons.rule: Some irregular verbs are rare but appear in books: seek → sought, weep → wept, forbid → forbade, bear → bore.

examples.text: They sought help from the teacher.

lessons.tip: If you are unsure, check a dictionary: it lists irregular past forms.

check.prompt: Choose: The king ___ anyone to enter.
check.explain: forbid → forbade in the past.

lessons.title: He, she, it + -s
lessons.rule: In the present simple, add -s or -es to the verb after he, she, it or one person or thing: she sings, he fixes, the dog barks.

examples.text: It rains a lot in July.

lessons.tip: I, you, we, they: no -s (they play).

check.prompt: Choose: She ___ to music every evening.
check.explain: she → add -s: listens.

lessons.title: Plural subjects
lessons.rule: A plural subject takes a plural verb: the mice run, the trees grow, my cousins live nearby.

examples.text: The birds are on the roof.

lessons.tip: Find the subject first, then match the verb to it.

check.explain: people is plural: are.

lessons.title: Two subjects with and
lessons.rule: Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb: Anil and Sara are friends.

examples.text: My sister and I walk to school.

examples.note: but a single dish can be singular

lessons.tip: and adds the subjects together, so the verb is plural.

check.prompt: Choose: Tom and his dog ___ in the park.
check.explain: Tom and his dog = two: are.

lessons.title: Words between subject and verb
lessons.rule: The verb agrees with the subject, not with a noun just before it: The jar of sweets is empty. The cup of tea is hot.

examples.text: The colour of the flowers is bright.
The boys in the team are tired.

lessons.tip: Cover the words between: 'The box … is'.

check.prompt: Choose: The basket of eggs ___ full.
check.explain: The subject is the basket (one): is.

lessons.title: Each, every, everyone
lessons.rule: each, every, everyone, nobody and somebody take a singular verb: Each of the girls has a ticket. Everyone is here.
lessons.tip: Each of the… is still one at a time: singular.

check.prompt: Choose: Each of the players ___ a shirt.
check.explain: each → singular: has.

lessons.title: either … or, neither … nor
lessons.rule: With either … or and neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the driver nor the passengers were hurt. Either the girls or their father is coming.

examples.text: Either my parents or my aunt is coming.
Neither the dog nor the cats were hungry.

lessons.tip: Look at the subject closest to the verb.

check.prompt: Choose: Neither Priya nor her brothers ___ at home.
check.explain: The nearer subject, brothers, is plural: are.

lessons.title: Inverted order; a number of
lessons.rule: When the verb comes first, find the subject after it: There are many birds. Here comes the bus. 'A number of' is plural; 'the number of' is singular.

examples.text: A number of shops were closed.
The number of cars is growing.

lessons.tip: Turn the sentence round: many birds are there.

check.prompt: Choose: There ___ three books on the desk.
check.explain: The subject is three books: are.

lessons.title: a or an
lessons.rule: Use an before a word that starts with a vowel (a, e, i, o, u) and a before a consonant: an orange, an egg, a ball, a cat.
lessons.tip: Say it aloud: 'an apple' is easier to say than 'a apple'.

check.explain: egg starts with a vowel: an egg.

lessons.title: a first, then the
lessons.rule: Use a when you first mention something, then the when you mention it again: I found a shell. The shell was pink. Use a before a job: He is a farmer.

examples.text: We bought a kite. The kite was red.

lessons.tip: a = one of many; the = the one we both know about.

check.explain: Use a or an before a job: an engineer.

lessons.title: a or an by sound
lessons.rule: Choose a or an by the first sound, not the first letter: an honour (silent h), an MP; a unicorn, a one-rupee coin (they start with 'yoo' and 'w' sounds).
lessons.tip: Listen to the sound at the start, not the letter.

check.explain: uniform starts with a 'yoo' sound: a uniform.

lessons.title: the for one of a kind
lessons.rule: Use the for things there is only one of, or that everyone knows: the moon, the sky, the Prime Minister.
lessons.tip: If there is only one, it is the.

check.explain: There is only one moon: the moon.

lessons.title: No a with uncountable nouns
lessons.rule: Some nouns cannot be counted: luggage, bread, water, news, rice. Do not use a or an with them: some luggage, a piece of bread.

examples.text: There is a lot of traffic today.

lessons.tip: If you cannot put a number in front of it, do not use a or an.

check.explain: help is uncountable here: some help.

lessons.title: General statements
lessons.rule: For general statements about all of something, use no article with plurals and abstract nouns: Elephants are strong. Kindness is important.
lessons.tip: Talking about all of them, in general? No article.

check.explain: A general, abstract idea: no article.

lessons.title: Articles with names
lessons.rule: Most names of people, cities and countries have no article (Delhi, India), but rivers, oceans and some countries do: the Yamuna, the Indian Ocean, the United States. Mountains do not: Mount Abu.
lessons.tip: Rivers, seas and oceans take the.

check.prompt: Choose: ___ Pacific is the largest ocean.
check.explain: Oceans take the: the Pacific.

lessons.title: Regular plurals
lessons.rule: Most nouns add -s for more than one; nouns ending in s, x, ch or sh add -es: cats, books, buses, boxes.
lessons.tip: Listen for the extra 'iz' sound: -es.

check.explain: glass ends in s, so add -es: glasses.

lessons.title: -ies and irregular plurals
lessons.rule: Consonant + y becomes -ies (baby → babies). Some plurals are irregular: child → children, mouse → mice, man → men, foot → feet.
lessons.tip: Never write childs or mouses.

check.explain: child is irregular: children.

lessons.title: many or much
lessons.rule: Use many with things you can count (many books) and much with things you cannot count (much water). A lot of works with both.

examples.text: How many apples? How much milk?

lessons.tip: Can you count it? many. Can't count it? much.

check.prompt: Choose: How ___ sugar do you want?
check.explain: sugar cannot be counted: much.

lessons.title: Uncountable nouns
lessons.rule: Some nouns have no plural and take a singular verb: information, advice, furniture, news, luggage. The news is good.
lessons.tip: To count them, use 'a piece of' or 'an item of'.

check.explain: news is uncountable and singular: is.

lessons.title: Both ways, and rare plurals
lessons.rule: Some nouns can be both: coffee (the drink) / two coffees (cups). Some plurals come from Latin or Greek: criterion → criteria, phenomenon → phenomena.
lessons.tip: criteria and phenomena are plurals: they take are.

check.explain: The singular is phenomenon.

lessons.title: Capitals: starts, I and names
lessons.rule: Use a capital letter at the start of a sentence, for the word I, and for names of people and pets.

examples.text: My friend Arjun and I play chess.

lessons.tip: I is always a capital, wherever it is in the sentence.

check.explain: Capitals for the start, for I and for the name Sita.

lessons.title: Capitals: days, months, places
lessons.rule: Days, months, festivals, cities, countries, rivers and languages start with a capital: Monday, June, Diwali, Chennai, India, Hindi.
lessons.tip: Seasons do not take capitals: summer, winter.

options: We go to mumbai in may.
We go to Mumbai in May.
We go to Mumbai in may.
check.explain: Mumbai (a city) and May (a month) both need capitals.

lessons.title: Capitals: titles and organisations
lessons.rule: Use capitals for titles (Dr Rao, Principal Mehta), organisations (Indian Railways) and adjectives from names (Indian, French). Do not capitalise ordinary nouns: my school, the river.

examples.text: Dr Sharma works at City Hospital.
We went to the river near our school.

lessons.tip: Is it the name of one particular thing? Capital. A general word? No capital.

options: My School is near the River.
My school is near the river.
my school is near the River.
check.explain: school and river are ordinary nouns here: no capitals.

lessons.title: Capitals: finer points
lessons.rule: Start quoted speech with a capital (She said, "We are late."). Capitalise a title before a name (Uncle Ravi) but not alone (my uncle). Capitalise the main words of book titles.

examples.text: Ask your aunt. Ask Aunt Leela.

lessons.tip: A title used as part of a name gets a capital.

check.explain: uncle is not part of a name here: no capital.

lessons.title: Apostrophes in short forms
lessons.rule: An apostrophe shows where letters are missing: do not → don't, I am → I'm, is not → isn't, it is → it's.
lessons.tip: Put the apostrophe exactly where the letters were taken out.

check.explain: The o of not is missing: didn't.

lessons.title: 's for belonging
lessons.rule: Add 's to show that something belongs to one person or thing: the girl's bag, Ravi's bike, the dog's bowl.
lessons.tip: Ask: whose is it? The answer gets 's.

check.explain: The pencil belongs to Meena: Meena's.

lessons.title: No apostrophe in plain plurals
lessons.rule: A plain plural or a verb never needs an apostrophe: mangoes for sale (not mango's), she sells books (not sell's).
lessons.tip: If nothing belongs to anything, there is no apostrophe.

check.explain: A plain plural has no apostrophe: tomatoes.

lessons.title: Plural belonging, and its
lessons.rule: For a plural ending in s, put the apostrophe after the s: the girls' bags (several girls). its (belonging to it) has no apostrophe; it's means it is.
lessons.tip: One girl: girl's. Many girls: girls'.

check.prompt: Which is correct? (bags of several boys)
check.explain: Several boys, so the apostrophe comes after the s: boys'.

lessons.title: Irregular plurals and joint belonging
lessons.rule: Plurals that do not end in s take 's: the children's toys, the people's choice. For two owners of one thing, put 's on the second: Ravi and Sita's house.
lessons.tip: children is already plural, so just add 's.

check.explain: children is plural without s, so add 's: children's.

lessons.title: Everyday words
lessons.rule: The most common words are the ones you meet every day. Knowing them well, including their different meanings, makes reading easier.
lessons.tip: When you meet a new word, say it, read the sentence again, and try using it.

check.prompt: Which word means the opposite of 'early'?
check.explain: early ↔ late.

lessons.title: Common words
lessons.rule: Words like 'borrow', 'journey' and 'gentle' are common in stories and everyday talk. The sentence around a word often shows its meaning.

examples.text: May I borrow your pen? (use it and give it back)
a long journey (a trip from one place to another)

lessons.tip: Look at the words around a new word for clues.

check.prompt: 'She spoke in a gentle voice.' gentle means:
check.explain: A gentle voice is soft and kind.

lessons.title: Words in everyday texts
lessons.rule: Newspapers, notices and school books use words like 'urgent', 'ancient' and 'encourage'. Learn them with an example sentence.

examples.text: The ancient temple is a thousand years old.

lessons.tip: Keep a list of new words with a sentence for each.

check.prompt: 'This is urgent' means it must be done:
check.explain: urgent: it needs attention now.

lessons.title: Less frequent words
lessons.rule: Secondary-school reading brings words like 'reluctant', 'abundant' and 'vivid'. Notice them, guess from context, then check.

examples.text: He was reluctant to leave (he did not want to).
an abundant harvest (a very large one)

lessons.tip: Guess, then check in a dictionary.

check.prompt: 'a vivid dream' is a dream that is:
check.explain: vivid means very clear and bright.

lessons.title: Words in textbooks
lessons.rule: Textbooks use general words such as 'significant', 'evident' and 'sufficient'. They make writing more precise.
lessons.tip: Try replacing the word with a simpler one to check you understand it.

check.explain: sufficient = enough.

lessons.title: Precise words
lessons.rule: Less common words carry exact meanings: 'meticulous' (very careful about details), 'candid' (honest and direct).
lessons.tip: Use a precise word only when you are sure of its meaning.

check.explain: meticulous: very careful about every detail.

lessons.title: Rare words
lessons.rule: Rare words like 'ephemeral' (lasting a very short time) are worth learning when they say exactly what you mean.
lessons.tip: Learn rare words in families: ubiquitous, ubiquity.

check.explain: ephemeral: lasting only a short time.

lessons.title: un- and re-
lessons.rule: un- means not or the opposite (unhappy, untie). re- means again or back (redo, refill, return).
lessons.tip: Cover the prefix to find the base word.

check.explain: re- means again.

lessons.title: dis-, mis-, pre-, over-
lessons.rule: dis- means not or the opposite (disagree), mis- means wrongly (misspell), pre- means before (preview), over- means too much (overcooked).
lessons.tip: Knowing the prefix gives you half the meaning.

check.explain: over- means too much.

lessons.title: Choosing the negative prefix
lessons.rule: im- comes before b, m and p (impossible, immature), il- before l (illegal), ir- before r (irregular), and in- or un- elsewhere (incorrect, unkind).
lessons.tip: Look at the first letter of the base word.

check.explain: legal starts with l, so il-: illegal.

lessons.title: sub- and inter-
lessons.rule: sub- means under or below (subway, submarine). inter- means between (international, interact).

examples.text: a submarine travels under the sea
an inter-school match is between schools

lessons.tip: inter- between; intra- within.

check.explain: inter- means between.

lessons.title: Prefixes in longer words
lessons.rule: Academic words often have prefixes: counter- (against: counterattack), semi- (half: semicircle), mis- (wrongly: misconception).

examples.text: semi-final: the round before the final

lessons.tip: Split the word: semi + circle.

check.explain: semi- means half.

lessons.title: -ful, -ly and -er
lessons.rule: -ful means full of (helpful), -ly often makes an adverb that says how (quickly), and -er can mean a person who does something (teacher, player).
lessons.tip: The suffix often tells you what kind of word it is.

check.explain: -er: a person who does it.

lessons.title: The right form for the place
lessons.rule: Use an adjective to describe a noun (a careful driver) and an adverb to describe a verb (she drives carefully).

examples.text: He is quick. He runs quickly.
a happy child; she smiled happily

lessons.tip: Describing how someone does something? Use the -ly word.

check.explain: It describes how she spoke: an adverb, confidently.

lessons.title: Making nouns
lessons.rule: -ness, -ment and -tion make nouns: kind → kindness, enjoy → enjoyment, invite → invitation.
lessons.tip: If you can put 'the' in front of it, it is probably a noun.

check.explain: improve + -ment = improvement.

lessons.title: Less regular forms
lessons.rule: Some word families change more: decide → decision, able → ability, explain → explanation.
lessons.tip: Learn the noun with the verb: decide, decision.

check.explain: decide → decision.

lessons.title: How a suffix changes meaning
lessons.rule: A suffix can change meaning: -able means can be (washable), -less means without (fearless), -ish means a little (reddish).
lessons.tip: Read the suffix as part of the meaning.

check.explain: -less means without.

lessons.title: Irregular abstract nouns
lessons.rule: Some abstract nouns change their spelling: maintain → maintenance, pronounce → pronunciation, explain → explanation.
lessons.tip: Learn the noun's spelling separately from the verb's.

check.explain: pronunciation: the o in -noun- drops.

lessons.title: Opposites
lessons.rule: Antonyms are words with opposite meanings: big / small, hot / cold, open / close, early / late.

examples.text: The bag is heavy; the box is light.
Push the door, then pull it.

lessons.tip: Learn opposites in pairs.

check.explain: empty ↔ full.

lessons.title: Same and opposite in a sentence
lessons.rule: Synonyms have the same or nearly the same meaning: begin / start, big / large. In a sentence, choose the one that keeps the meaning.

examples.text: The film will begin (start) at six.
a generous (kind, giving) person ↔ a selfish one

lessons.tip: Swap the word in and read the sentence again.

check.prompt: A word that means the same as 'start':
check.explain: start = begin.

lessons.title: Less common pairs
lessons.rule: Learn synonyms and opposites for less common words: narrow ↔ wide, reluctant = unwilling, ancient ↔ modern.

examples.text: a narrow road ↔ a wide road

lessons.tip: Think of a sentence where both words fit.

check.prompt: A word that means the same as 'reluctant':
check.explain: reluctant = unwilling.

lessons.title: The word that fits
lessons.rule: Near-synonyms are not always interchangeable. Tired and exhausted are close, but exhausted is much stronger; a fragile vase breaks easily.

examples.text: After the race, she was exhausted.
Handle the fragile glass with care.

lessons.tip: Ask which word fits the strength and situation of the sentence.

check.explain: Very tired after great effort: exhausted.

lessons.title: Fine differences
lessons.rule: Some near-synonyms show an attitude: determined (good) / stubborn (not so good); thrifty (careful with money) / stingy (unwilling to share). glance (a quick look) / stare (a long look).
lessons.tip: Ask: does the word praise or criticise?

check.prompt: Which word praises someone careful with money?
check.explain: thrifty praises; stingy criticises.

lessons.title: Finding a fact
lessons.rule: To answer a who, what, where or when question, find the sentence that answers it. The answer is written in the text.

examples.text: Text: "Ravi keeps his cricket bat under his bed." Question: Where is the bat? Answer: under his bed.
examples.note: worked example: the sentence tells us

examples.text: Where needs a place. Who needs a person. When needs a time.

lessons.tip: Read the question first, then look back in the text for the answer.

check.prompt: Text: "Nisha's cat is called Snowy. Snowy is black." What colour is Snowy?
check.explain: The text says 'Snowy is black'. The name sounds white, but the text tells us the colour.

lessons.title: Finding details in a longer text
lessons.rule: In a longer text, use the question to find the right paragraph first, then the right sentence.

examples.text: Question: What did they eat for lunch? Look for the paragraph about lunch, then the sentence with the food.

lessons.tip: Look for a word from the question, then read the whole sentence around it.

check.prompt: Text: "In the morning we swam in the river. In the afternoon we ate rice and dal under a tree." What did they eat?
check.explain: The afternoon sentence tells us: rice and dal.

lessons.title: Words that look right
lessons.rule: Some answers repeat words from the text but do not answer the question. Check that your answer really answers it.

examples.text: Text: "The party was planned for Sunday, but it rained, so it was held on Monday." When was the party held? Answer: Monday. Sunday was only the plan.

lessons.tip: Ask: does this answer the question, or does it just use the same words?

check.prompt: Text: "We wanted to go to the beach, but the car broke down, so we went to the park." Where did they go?
check.explain: They wanted the beach, but they went to the park.

lessons.title: What is it mostly about?
lessons.rule: The topic is what the whole text is about. Choose the answer that fits every sentence, not just one.

examples.text: A text gives a dog's name, what it eats and where it sleeps. It is mostly about the dog, not about its food.

lessons.tip: A detail is true, but too small. The topic covers everything.

check.prompt: Text: "Our school has a big library. It has books about animals, space and stories. We can borrow two books a week." What is it mostly about?
check.explain: Every sentence is about the library; the others are details.

lessons.title: Choosing the best title
lessons.rule: A good title fits the whole story. A title made from one detail is usually too small.

examples.text: Story: a boy loses his shoe, looks everywhere, and his dog brings it back. Best title: The Dog Who Found the Shoe, not A Red Shoe.

lessons.tip: Say the story in one sentence. The best title matches that sentence.

check.prompt: Text: "Ana's balloon flew away. She cried. Her friend shared his balloon, and they played together." Best title?
check.explain: The story is about the friend's kindness.

lessons.title: The main idea of a paragraph
lessons.rule: Each paragraph has one big idea. The other sentences give details about it. Find the idea the other sentences support.

examples.text: "Frogs live in many places. Some live in ponds, some in trees, and some even in deserts." Main idea: frogs live in many places.

lessons.tip: If you can say 'for example' before a sentence, it is a detail.

check.prompt: Text: "Plants need light. Without light, their leaves turn yellow. A plant left in a dark cupboard soon dies." Main idea?
check.explain: The other sentences show why plants need light.
